a: a festival of the Jews
p: John does not name it. Readers have guessed Passover, Pentecost, Booths, Trumpets and Purim.
b: Every other festival in John is named: Passover (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), Booths (7:2) and Dedication (10:22). Here it is only "a festival." A few manuscripts add "the," which would point to the chief festival, Passover or Booths (see the variant). Irenaeus counted it as one of Jesus's Passovers, which lengthens his ministry. Others have proposed Pentecost, Trumpets (the New Year) or Purim. Nothing in the chapter settles it. What matters to John is that it is a Sabbath (5:9) during a pilgrim feast, when Jerusalem was crowded and Jesus is again in the city of the Temple authorities.

a: the Sheep Gate
p: A gate in the north wall of the Temple area, rebuilt in Nehemiah's day, probably where sacrificial sheep came in.
b: The Greek says only "by the sheep (place)," and the KJV filled the gap with "market." Most read "gate," because Nehemiah names a Sheep Gate just north of the Temple (Nehemiah 3:1, 32; 12:39). Sheep for the sacrifices were probably brought in that way. The pool lay just outside it, north of the Temple Mount, in the district Josephus calls Bezetha, the "New City." John is the only Gospel writer who names places like this, and archaeology has confirmed several of them.

a: in Hebrew
p: The Greek word means "in the Jews' language," which in Jesus's day usually meant Aramaic.
b: Hebraisti can mean Hebrew proper, but in John it labels names like Gabbatha and Golgotha (19:13, 17), which are Aramaic. Jews in first-century Judea spoke Aramaic day to day and read Hebrew in worship, and both are "the Hebrew language" to a Greek speaker. So many English Bibles say "Aramaic" here. The Plain English Translation keeps "Hebrew" because that is what the Greek says and the Greek writer did not separate the two.

a: It has five covered porches.
p: Digging near St. Anne's Church found two large pools with a dam between them. How the five porches stood is debated.
b: Augustine read the five porches as the five books of Moses, and some critics in the 1800s doubted the pool existed at all. Then excavations beside St. Anne's Church, north of the Temple Mount, uncovered two large rock-cut pools separated by a wall or dam, with column pieces, and to the east small baths and caves. Most scholars, following Joachim Jeremias, reconstruct colonnades on the four sides and one along the dam, which would make five. Others, such as Shimon Gibson, doubt the portico on the dam and read the southern pool as a large stepped pool for ritual bathing. In the Roman city built after AD 135 the site held a shrine of Asclepius, the Greek god of healing. A Dead Sea Scroll on copper (3Q15) seems to name a place "Beth Eshdatayin," "the house of the two outflows," perhaps the twin pools. The present tense, "there is," may hint that John wrote before AD 70, or may be a storyteller's present.

a: thirty-eight years
p: Israel wandered thirty-eight years before it crossed into the land. Some readers see the echo; most see a plain fact.
b: The number shows the case is hopeless: the man has been ill longer than many people then lived. Deuteronomy uses the same figure for Israel's lost years: "From the time we left Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the Zered Valley was thirty-eight years" (Deuteronomy 2:14). Some interpreters see the healed man as a picture of Israel, stuck at the edge of the promise. Augustine read the number as forty, the number of fulfilled law, lacking two, love for God and love for neighbor. Most modern commentators think John simply records the length of the illness.

a: Do you want to become healthy?
p: Why ask a man who has waited for years whether he wants to be well?
b: The question sounds unnecessary, and the man does not answer it. He explains why he has not been healed instead. Some readers hear a real question: long illness can make a person settle into it, and healing would change his whole life, including how he earned a living by begging. Others see the Johannine pattern where Jesus starts the conversation and the other person answers at a lower level (3:4; 4:11). In this story, unlike most Gospel healings, nobody asks Jesus for help and the man shows no faith. The healing is Jesus's own free act.

a: when the water gets stirred
p: The sick believed the first one in after the water stirred would be healed. Later copies added an angel to explain it.
b: Perhaps channels or runoff moved the water from time to time. The sick man shares the popular belief that the first one in would be cured. Many later manuscripts add an explanation: an angel came down at certain times and stirred the water (see the variant at 5:4). The oldest manuscripts lack it, and most scholars think a copyist added an existing local belief to explain 5:7. Tertullian, about AD 200, already knew the story of the angel. John's point is the contrast: the man waits for a race he can never win, and Jesus heals him with a word, no water needed.

a: Stand up, lift up your mat and walk.
t: The same words as in Mark
p: Jesus's command matches Mark 2:9 almost word for word: rise, take your mat, walk.
b: The Greek krabattos is a poor person's pallet, light enough to roll up and carry. Mark tells a similar healing in Capernaum, where Jesus says "rise, take up your mat" with the same rare word (Mark 2:9; compare Mark 2:11). Some scholars think the two stories share a common tradition. The differences are large, though: Mark's man is let down through a roof by four friends and Jesus first forgives his sins, while John's man is alone and the problem is the Sabbath. Either way, carrying the mat is the proof that the healing is real, and here it becomes the cause of the trouble.

a: So the Jews kept saying
p: In this scene "the Jews" are the Jerusalem authorities. The healed man, also a Jew, reports to them.
b: John uses hoi Ioudaioi about seventy times, and it does not always mean the same thing (see 1:19). Here it cannot mean the Jewish people as a whole: the healed man and the crowd are Jewish, and the man "reported to the Jews" (5:15), so they are a group with authority in the Temple. Most scholars think John means the religious leaders in Jerusalem. The Plain English Translation keeps the Greek word, as this site does throughout John, and the notes say who is meant. In chapter 6 the same word is used of a crowd of Galileans (6:41).

a: You are not allowed to carry the mat.
p: The Law and the prophets forbade carrying loads on the Sabbath. Later Jewish law made it one of 39 kinds of work.
b: The ban on carrying comes from Jeremiah 17:21–22 and Nehemiah, who shut the gates "so that no load would come in on the Sabbath day" (Nehemiah 13:19). The Mishnah, written down about AD 200 but reflecting older debates, lists carrying from one domain to another among the 39 main kinds of forbidden work. It also discusses a related case: a person who carries a living person on a bed is not guilty even for the bed, since the bed is secondary to the person. Carrying an empty bed falls under the general rule. So by the standards of the time the authorities were right that the man was carrying a load. Jesus does not deny it; he answers with a claim about God (5:17).
r: Jeremiah 17:21–22; Nehemiah 13:15–19; Exodus 20:10; Mark 2:23–28; Mishnah Shabbat 7:2; Mishnah Shabbat 10:5

a: Do not keep on sinning, so that nothing worse comes on you.
t: Was his illness caused by sin?
p: Jesus warns him, but in chapter 9 he denies that a man's blindness came from sin. How do the two fit?
b: The Greek is a present command, "stop sinning" or "do not go on sinning." Some read it as showing that this man's illness was the result of a particular sin. Others note that Jesus says nothing of the past and warns only of "something worse," most likely final judgment (5:29), which is worse than thirty-eight years of illness. In 9:2–3 Jesus flatly rejects the idea that the man born blind suffered for his own or his parents' sin. Read together, the passages teach that sin can bring harm, but that no one may read a person's sins from his suffering. Compare Mark 2:5, where forgiveness and healing come together.

a: reported to the Jews
p: Did the man betray Jesus, or simply tell who had healed him?
b: Readers have judged the healed man very differently. Some see him as ungrateful: he never thanks Jesus, blames him when questioned (5:11), and goes straight to the authorities, setting off the plot of 5:16–18. Others think he innocently answers the question the leaders had asked (5:12), perhaps even bearing witness. John does not say. On the contrast with the man born blind in chapter 9, see the chapter page.

a: My Father is at work right up to now
t: Does God rest on the Sabbath?
p: Jewish teachers asked how God could keep the Sabbath and still run the world. Jesus's answer uses that debate.
b: Genesis says God rested on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2–3). Yet the world goes on: babies are born and people die on the Sabbath. Philo of Alexandria wrote that God never stops making things. Later rabbinic writings say God works on the Sabbath only in giving life and in judging (Genesis Rabbah 11:10), and tell how four rabbis in Rome explained that God may "carry" within his own house, the whole world (Exodus Rabbah 30:9). Jesus's claim is that he shares the work God does even on the Sabbath, giving life and judging, which is exactly what 5:21–22 go on to say. The hearers understood that he was claiming God's own right (5:18).

a: making himself equal to God
p: John's opponents say Jesus makes himself equal to God. The rest of the chapter answers: the Son does nothing on his own.
b: To call God "my Father" was not itself shocking; Jews prayed to God as Father. What angered the hearers was "his own Father" (idios) together with the claim to share God's Sabbath work. Readers differ on what John thinks of the charge. Most Christian interpreters, and the creeds, hold that John agrees with it in his own way: Jesus is equal to God (1:1; 10:30; 20:28), yet not a man making himself God, but the Son who does nothing on his own (5:19, 30). The fathers used the verse against Arius. Others read 5:18 as the opponents' accusation, which Jesus answers in 5:19 by denying that he acts on his own; this is the reading of Unitarians and Jehovah's Witnesses, as it was of the Arians. Some scholars read 5:19–30 as the language of agency: one who is sent acts with the sender's full authority without being the sender (Peder Borgen). Jewish scholars such as Adele Reinhartz think the conflict reflects arguments between church and synagogue in John's day, and Daniel Boyarin argues that some Jews then could already think of a second divine figure beside God.

a: the Son is not able to do anything on his own
p: Behind 5:19–20 may be a picture from daily life: a son learning his father's trade by watching.
b: C. H. Dodd suggested that these verses contain a "hidden parable." In a village workshop, a son does not invent his own methods. He watches his father, copies what he sees, and the father, who loves him, shows him all his secrets. Jesus applies this to himself. Read this way, "not able to do anything on his own" is not weakness but perfect agreement. The fathers of the church debated these words. Arians read them as proof that the Son is lesser. Athanasius, Hilary and Augustine answered that the Son receives everything from the Father, his being included, and so does all the Father does, "in the same way."

a: The Father raises up the dead and makes them alive
p: Giving life to the dead was what Scripture and Jewish prayer said only God could do.
b: "I kill, and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39); "The LORD kills and makes alive" (1 Samuel 2:6). The daily Jewish prayer called the Amidah, or Eighteen Benedictions, praises God as the one "who gives life to the dead," and its early form probably goes back to the first century. So when Jesus says the Son "makes alive anyone he wishes," he claims a power Jews reserved for God. He does it now by his word (5:24–25) and on the last day by raising the dead (5:28–29). Chapter 11 acts this out with Lazarus.

a: He has already moved out of death and into life.
t: Eternal life now, and resurrection later
p: 5:24–25 speak of life already present; 5:28–29 of a future resurrection. Scholars disagree about how they fit.
b: Verse 24 says the believer "has" eternal life and "has already moved" from death to life. Verse 25 says the hour "has arrived now." This is often called realized eschatology: the life of the age to come is present in Jesus. Then verses 28–29 describe a future day when the dead in their tombs will rise. Rudolf Bultmann thought a later church editor added the future verses to correct John. Most scholars today think John held both together on purpose: the life begins now, and the body is raised later. The same pairing comes in 6:40, 54 and 11:24–26.

a: since he is the Son of Man
t: "The Son of Man" or "a son of man"?
p: Only here in the Gospels does the title lack "the" in Greek. It echoes Daniel 7.
b: Everywhere else in the Gospels Jesus calls himself ho huios tou anthrōpou, "the Son of Man." Here it is huios anthrōpou with no article, exactly the wording of Daniel 7:13 in Greek, where "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds and is given authority, honor and a kingdom. So most readers hear Daniel's figure: the Father gives judgment to the one Daniel saw. Others stress the plain sense, "because he is a human being": humanity will be judged by one who shares it. Some early writers read it this way. The Plain English Translation follows this site's rule and prints the title, "the Son of Man," and this note gives the other sense. Many commentators, such as Carson, add a point of grammar: a definite noun placed before the verb "to be" often drops the article in Greek, so the missing "the" may mean nothing at all.

a: a resurrection that brings judgment
p: The words reuse Daniel 12:2: some will wake to life, some to shame.
b: Daniel 12:2 is the Old Testament's clearest promise of resurrection: "many of those sleeping in the dusty ground will wake, some to the life of the age, and some to disgrace and to contempt of the age" (Daniel 12:2, translated here from the Hebrew). Jesus widens it to "everyone in the tombs." The two outcomes are named by deeds, "those who did good" and "those who did wicked things." Since 5:24 ties life to believing, readers have asked how faith and deeds relate here. See the card "Where Christians differ" on this chapter's page.

a: my testimony does not hold true
t: Why his own word is not enough
p: "True" here is a court word: valid evidence. One witness alone could not settle a case.
b: The Law required more than one witness: "A matter is to stand on the word of two witnesses or on the word of three witnesses" (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jewish law also held that a person could not testify on his own behalf. So Jesus grants his opponents' rule and then names other witnesses: John the Baptist, his works, the Father and the Scriptures. In 8:13–14 he will say the opposite, that his testimony is true even about himself, because he knows where he came from. The two sayings answer different questions: whether the evidence meets the legal standard, and whether what he says is in fact true.
orig: ἡ μαρτυρία μου οὐκ ἔστιν ἀληθής

a: the lamp that burns and gives off light
p: John was a lamp, not the light (1:8). The image may echo the lamp God prepared for his anointed one.
b: The prologue already said that John was not himself the light (1:8). A lamp burns and gives light for a while and then goes out, as John's ministry did. Some hear Psalm 132:17: "I have set a lamp in order for my anointed one," which would make John the lamp that goes before the Messiah. Sirach 48:1 describes Elijah, with whom John was linked (Matthew 11:14), as a prophet whose word "burned like a lamp." The past tense "was" suggests that John was already in prison or dead.

a: Not once have you heard his voice.
p: At Sinai Israel heard God's voice but saw no form. Jesus says these hearers have neither.
b: Moses reminded Israel: "You were hearing the sound of words, but you were seeing no form. There was nothing but a voice" (Deuteronomy 4:12). Jesus's hearers claim to stand in that tradition, yet he says they have not heard God's voice or seen his form. "Form" is eidos, the word of Deuteronomy 4:12 in the Greek Old Testament. In John only the Son has seen the Father (1:18; 6:46), and whoever has seen Jesus has seen the Father (14:9). So the Father's "testimony" is not a separate voice from heaven. It comes in Jesus himself, his works, and the Scriptures that point to him.

a: You dig into the Scriptures
p: The Greek verb has the same form for "you search" and "search!" The KJV made it a command.
b: Eraunate can be read either way. The KJV and many old sermons take it as a command: "Search the scriptures." Most modern translations take it as a statement, because the next words, "because you think you will have eternal life in them," describe what the hearers already do. Jesus does not mock their study. The rabbis said, "The more Torah, the more life" (Mishnah Avot 2:7). His complaint is that study which does not lead to him misses the Scriptures' own point.

a: If another man comes in his own name
t: Who is the other who comes?
p: Readers have seen false messiahs, the leader of a later revolt, or the Antichrist.
b: Jesus contrasts himself, sent by the Father and rejected, with someone who will come on his own authority and be welcomed. Some think of the many would-be messiahs of the first century, such as those Josephus describes. Others think of Simon bar Kosiba (Bar Kokhba), hailed as messiah in the revolt of AD 132–135, though John was written before that. Irenaeus and other early writers applied the verse to the Antichrist at the end. Many modern readers take it as a general saying: people accept a leader who flatters them sooner than one sent by God.

a: The one bringing charges against you is Moses
p: In Jewish tradition Moses was Israel's great defender before God. Here he becomes the prosecutor.
b: Moses pleaded for Israel after the golden calf (Exodus 32:11–14, 30–32), and later Jewish writings, such as the Testament of Moses, picture him as Israel's appointed intercessor (Testament of Moses 11:17; 12:6). Jesus turns this around. The one they trust to speak for them will speak against them, because his writings point to Jesus and they refuse to listen. Deuteronomy itself had said the scroll of the law would stand "as a witness against you" (Deuteronomy 31:26). This is an argument inside Judaism about who reads Moses rightly, not a rejection of Moses.
r: Exodus 32:11–14; Exodus 32:30–32; Deuteronomy 31:26; Testament of Moses 11:17; Testament of Moses 12:6; 1:17; 9:28–29

a: it was about me that he wrote
t: What did Moses write about Jesus?
p: Jesus does not name a verse. The likeliest is the promised prophet like Moses.
b: The strongest candidate is Deuteronomy 18:15: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers. You must listen to him." John's crowds connect Jesus with "the Prophet" (1:21; 6:14; 7:40). Other candidates are the manna and the bronze snake (Numbers 21:9; compare John 3:14), the Passover lamb (19:36) and the promises to Abraham (8:56). Jesus may mean the whole of the Torah, read as a story that leads to him (Luke 24:27).

a: the Sea of Tiberias
t: Sea of Galilee, Sea of Tiberias
p: Herod Antipas founded Tiberias on the lake's west shore about AD 20, naming it for the emperor Tiberius.
b: The lake goes by several names: the Sea of Galilee, the Lake of Gennesaret (Luke 5:1), Kinneret in the Old Testament (Numbers 34:11), and the Sea of Tiberias, which only John uses (here and 21:1). The city of Tiberias was built by Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, and named after the Roman emperor. The name of the lake came to be used later in the century, so John's double name helps readers outside the land know which lake he means. The Gospels never say that Jesus entered Tiberias.

a: It was close to the Passover
p: John mentions three Passovers, which is where the idea of a three-year ministry comes from.
b: Matthew, Mark and Luke mention only the final Passover. John names three (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), and perhaps a fourth if 5:1 was one, so tradition says Jesus taught for about three years. Here the date also gives the meaning. Passover remembered the exodus, and the chapter is full of it: Jesus goes up "the mountain" with his disciples (6:3), as Moses went up Sinai, a crowd in the wilderness, bread given from heaven, people complaining, a crossing of the sea, and finally flesh and blood. Because the feeding falls at Passover, many readers also hear the Last Supper, which John does not narrate in the usual way.

a: He said to Philip, "Where can we buy loaves
p: Jesus's question recalls Moses in the wilderness: "Where am I to get meat to give this whole people?"
b: Philip came from Bethsaida (1:44), near the place of the feeding (Luke 9:10), so he might know where bread could be bought. In Numbers 11:13 Moses asks the LORD, "Where am I to get meat to give this whole people?" and in Numbers 11:22 he doubts that enough could ever be found. Philip's answer in 6:7 sounds the same way. The story has begun to retell the wilderness, with Jesus in the place of the God who feeds his people.

a: Loaves costing two hundred denarii
p: A denarius was a day's pay for a laborer, so this was most of a year's wages.
b: The denarius was a silver Roman coin. In Matthew 20:2 an owner agrees to pay vineyard workers one denarius for a day. Two hundred denarii would be about two-thirds of a year's work for a day laborer, more than the disciples had. Mark gives the same sum (Mark 6:37). Philip's arithmetic is correct, and it is the point: there is no human way to feed this crowd.

a: five loaves of barley bread
p: Barley bread was the food of the poor. Only John says the loaves were barley, as in Elisha's miracle.
b: Wheat was the better grain; barley was cheaper and fed the poor and animals. Barley ripened first, and its firstfruits were offered at Passover time, so the detail fits the season (6:4). John alone mentions it, and it recalls 2 Kings 4:42–44. There a man brings Elisha "twenty barley loaves," his servant asks how this can feed a hundred men, and Elisha says, "They will eat, and there will be extra." In John a boy brings fewer loaves, the crowd is fifty times bigger, and the leftovers fill twelve baskets: one greater than Elisha is here.

a: two small fish
p: The Greek word means fish eaten with bread, often dried or salted.
b: Opsarion is a diminutive of opson, any relish eaten with bread, and in John it means fish (also 21:9–13). On the lake, small fish were salted and dried for sale. The town of Magdala was known in Greek as Taricheae, from the word for salted fish. A boy might carry a few with his barley bread as a day's food. The other Gospels use the ordinary word for fish.

a: Make the people recline.
p: People reclined for a meal or a banquet. Spring grass fits the Passover season.
b: Jesus has the crowd lie down as guests did at a formal meal. The grass fits early spring, when the Galilean hills are green, as Mark's "green grass" also says (Mark 6:39). Some hear Psalm 23 here, where the shepherd makes his flock lie down in green pastures. John counts the men (andres) at about five thousand, as all four Gospels do. Matthew adds that women and children were not counted (Matthew 14:21). This is the only miracle of Jesus told in all four Gospels.

a: after giving thanks
t: A meal that sounds like the Lord's Supper
p: "Gave thanks" is the Greek word behind "Eucharist." Readers disagree on how much John intends the link.
b: The other Gospels say Jesus "blessed" the bread and broke it. John uses eucharisteō, "give thanks," which Christians soon used for the Lord's Supper, and repeats it in 6:23. He took, gave thanks, and gave out, as at the Last Supper (1 Corinthians 11:23–24), at Passover time (6:4). Many readers, ancient and modern, think John means the feeding to point ahead to the Eucharist and the bread talk of 6:51–58. Others answer that giving thanks before a meal was ordinary Jewish practice and that John makes no further sacramental hint here.

a: so that nothing will be lost
p: "So that nothing will be lost" prepares for 6:39: Jesus will lose none of those the Father gives him.
b: Jews did not waste bread, and gathering the leftovers proves how much food there was. But John's wording, "so that nothing will be lost" (apolētai), comes back in 6:39 ("I should not lose any of it") and 17:12, where it is people who are not lost. The early Christian prayer book called the Didache prays at the Lord's Supper over the "broken bread" (klasma, John's word for the pieces): as the grain once scattered on the hills was gathered into one loaf, so may the church be gathered from the ends of the earth.

a: twelve baskets
p: One basket for each of the Twelve, or for each tribe of Israel.
b: The kophinos was a sturdy wicker basket, the kind Roman writers associate with Jews on the road. All four Gospels have twelve, and Mark keeps the word separate from the seven larger baskets of the second feeding (Mark 8:19–20). Many readers see the twelve tribes: God's people are fed in full. Others think of the twelve disciples, who each gathered one. The number certainly shows there was more left over than there was at the start.

a: the Prophet, the one coming into the world
p: Bread in the wilderness made the crowd think of Moses, and of the prophet like him whom Moses promised.
b: Moses had promised a prophet like himself (Deuteronomy 18:15). See the note on 5:46. By Jesus's time some Jews expected this Prophet in the last days (1:21; 7:40), and the Samaritans looked for a coming one they called the Taheb. After a miracle that recalls the manna, the crowd draws the obvious conclusion. Josephus tells of other men in the first century who promised Moses-like signs in the wilderness and gathered crowds. John agrees that Jesus is the Prophet, but he will show that Jesus is more.

a: grab him to make him king
p: Galilean crowds wanted a leader to drive out Rome. Jesus refuses that kind of kingship.
b: After Herod the Great died in 4 BC, several men in Galilee and Judea had themselves proclaimed king, Josephus reports, and gathered armed followers. A prophet who could feed thousands in the wilderness looked like the king Israel was waiting for. The verb means to seize or snatch. Jesus withdraws. He is a king (1:49; 12:13; 18:37), but he tells Pilate his kingdom does not come from this world (18:36). Mark says only that Jesus made his disciples get into the boat quickly and sent the crowd away (Mark 6:45); John may explain why.

a: as he walked on the sea
p: In Scripture only God walks on the sea. Readers take the story as a miracle, a symbol, or a misunderstanding.
b: Job says of God, "Alone he spreads out the skies / and tramples on the back of the Sea" (Job 9:8), and a psalm says, "Your road was in the sea" (Psalm 77:19). Matthew and Mark tell the same event (Matthew 14:22–33; Mark 6:45–52). Most Christians read it as a real miracle that shows who Jesus is. Some scholars treat it as a story shaped by these psalms to teach that Jesus shares God's rule over chaos. The rationalist H. E. G. Paulus (1800s) argued that epi tēs thalassēs can mean "by the sea," as in 21:1, so the frightened disciples saw Jesus on the shore. The phrase can mean that, but John says the boat was far out (6:19) and the disciples were afraid, so most reject the idea.
r: Job 9:8; Psalm 77:19; Psalm 107:23–30; Isaiah 43:16; Matthew 14:22–33; Mark 6:45–52

a: I am. Stop being afraid.
p: Egō eimi can mean simply "It's me," but in Isaiah's Greek it is how God names himself.
b: On a dark sea the words could just identify a familiar voice: "It is I." Mark has the same two Greek words in the same story (Mark 6:50). But John often lets egō eimi stand alone with a deeper sense (8:24, 28, 58; 13:19; 18:5–8). In the Greek of Isaiah, God says the bare egō eimi, "I am," of himself (Isaiah 43:10, 25; 45:18; 46:4), and in Exodus 3:14 the Greek has "I am the one who is." Here, on the waters where only God walks, many readers hear both senses at once. The Plain English Translation keeps the bare "I am" so English readers can hear the echo, as this site does throughout John.

a: at once the boat was at the shore
p: John adds a detail the others lack: the boat arrived at once. It recalls the psalm of sailors saved by God.
b: "They wanted to take him into the boat" may mean that they did, or that before they could, the boat was already ashore. Either way the arrival is sudden. Psalm 107 tells of sailors in a storm who cried to the LORD, and "he steered them to the port they longed for" (Psalm 107:30). Some readers count this as a second miracle; others think John only means the rest of the trip passed quickly.

a: once the Lord had given thanks
p: John's narrator rarely calls Jesus "the Lord" before the resurrection. He does so here, at the meal.
b: Characters call Jesus kyrie ("sir" or "Lord") often, but the narrator himself uses "the Lord" before Easter only here and in 11:2 (and at 4:1 in some manuscripts). After the resurrection it becomes common (20:20; 21:7, 12). Repeating "given thanks" and calling Jesus "the Lord" makes the meal sound like the church's thanksgiving meal. Some manuscripts leave out the phrase; see the variant.

a: God the Father has marked him with his seal
p: A seal marked ownership and authority. God has set his mark on the Son.
b: In the ancient world a seal pressed into clay or wax showed who owned something and that it was genuine. The Father has "sealed" the Son: he has put his stamp of approval on him, and so his gift can be trusted. Many interpreters connect the sealing with Jesus's baptism, when the Spirit came down and remained on him (1:32–34). Others connect it with the signs, the Father's own proof. Compare 3:33, where whoever accepts Jesus's testimony "seals" that God is true.

a: Here is the work of God
p: They ask about works (plural); Jesus answers with one work: to believe.
b: The crowd asks what they must do. Jesus does not give a list of deeds. The one "work of God" is to keep believing in the one God sent. Readers have argued over the phrase. Augustine and the Reformers took it as a work God does in a person, not a work done to earn salvation. Catholic teaching agrees that faith is God's gift and adds that believing is also a free human act, moved by grace, from which good works grow. Either way, Jesus points the question about doing away from a program and toward a person. The Greek verb is in the present tense, "keep on believing"; the Byzantine text has a one-time form, "come to believe." Both are possible here, so the Plain English Translation says simply "believe."

a: 'Bread from heaven he gave them to eat.'
p: The words are closest to Psalm 78:24 in Greek. Exodus 16 and Nehemiah 9:15 say nearly the same.
b: The crowd's quotation combines several verses. Psalm 78:24 in the Greek Septuagint says "he gave them bread of heaven." This site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads "He made manna fall like rain on them for food. / He gave them heaven's grain." Exodus 16:4 has the LORD say, "I am about to make bread fall like rain from the sky for you," and Exodus 16:15 adds "That is the bread which the LORD has given you for your food." Nehemiah 9:15 is closest in English order: "Bread from the heavens you gave them." Peder Borgen argued that 6:31–58 works like a Jewish sermon on this one text, explaining it phrase by phrase: "bread," "from heaven," "he gave," "to eat."
r: Psalm 78:24; Exodus 16:4; Exodus 16:15; Nehemiah 9:15; Wisdom of Solomon 16:20

a: It was manna that our fathers ate in the desert
p: Some Jews expected the Messiah to bring back the manna. The crowd asks Jesus to match Moses.
b: The crowd has just eaten miraculous bread, yet they ask for a sign. Their point is that Moses gave bread every day for forty years, not once. Jewish writings voice a hope that the manna would return. 2 Baruch, from about AD 100, says that in the Messiah's time "the treasury of manna will again come down from on high." A later midrash says, "As the first redeemer brought down manna, so the last redeemer will bring down manna" (Ecclesiastes Rabbah 1:9). The crowd wants that sign. Jesus answers that he is the bread.

a: Moses has not given you the bread from heaven
p: Jesus does not deny the manna. He corrects who gave it and says the true bread is still being given.
b: Jesus makes two corrections. The giver was not Moses but God, as Exodus itself said (Exodus 16:15). And the tense changes: Moses "has not given," my Father "gives," now. Jewish teachers also said the manna was God's gift, and some linked it with the Torah, the bread of the mind (Philo; compare Deuteronomy 8:3). So Jesus's claim is not that Judaism was wrong about the manna. It is that the true bread from heaven, which the manna pointed to, is now present.

a: God's bread is what comes down out of heaven
t: "What comes down" or "he who comes down"?
p: The Greek can mean the bread that comes down or the person who comes down. John keeps both open until 6:35.
b: Ho katabainōn is masculine. Since artos, "bread," is also masculine, the phrase can mean "the bread that comes down" or "the one who comes down." The crowd hears bread (6:34). Readers who know 3:13 ("the Son of Man, who came down from heaven") hear a person. Jesus settles it two verses later: "I am the bread of life." The Plain English Translation's "what comes down" keeps the crowd's level for now.

a: I am the bread of life.
t: The first "I am" with a picture
p: Seven times Jesus says "I am" with an image: bread, light, gate, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine.
b: This is the first of John's seven "I am" sayings with a predicate: the bread of life (6:35), the light of the world (8:12), the gate (10:7), the good shepherd (10:11), the resurrection and the life (11:25), the way, the truth and the life (14:6), and the true vine (15:1). In Proverbs, Wisdom invites the simple, "Come, have some of my bread" (Proverbs 9:5), and Sirach has Wisdom say, "those who eat me will hunger for more" (Sirach 24:21). Jesus outdoes Wisdom: whoever comes to him "will not go hungry at all." Isaiah 55:1–3 also offers food and drink without cost to all who come and listen.

a: Everything the Father gives me
p: The Greek is neuter: "all that" the Father gives. It treats the believers as one whole.
b: John says pan ho, "everything that," not "everyone who." The same neuter returns in 6:39 ("I should not lose any of it") and 17:2, 24. It pictures those the Father gives as one gift, the whole people of God. The second half of the verse switches to the individual: "anyone who comes to me." The verse holds both together: God's giving, and each person's coming. How those relate is debated; see the card "Where Christians differ" on this chapter's page.
orig: πᾶν ὃ δίδωσίν μοι ὁ πατήρ

a: should raise it up on the last day
p: Four times in this chapter Jesus promises to raise believers on the last day.
b: The refrain comes in 6:39, 40, 44 and 54. Martha uses the same words in 11:24, and Jesus answers that he himself is the resurrection. The phrase is the language of Jewish hope for a final day of judgment and resurrection (Daniel 12:2, 13). It shows that the "eternal life" believers have now (6:47) does not cancel a future bodily resurrection. On the relation of present and future, see the note on 5:24.

a: So the Jews started complaining about him
t: Complaining in the wilderness, complaining in Capernaum
p: The verb is the one used of Israel complaining about food in the wilderness. And these "Jews" are Galileans.
b: Gongyzō is the Greek Old Testament's word for Israel's complaints in Exodus 16: "the whole community of Israelites complained against Moses and Aaron" (Exodus 16:2). The same people who asked for manna now complain like their ancestors. Note who they are: a crowd in a Galilean synagogue (6:59) who know Jesus's family (6:42), not the Jerusalem authorities of chapter 5. Many readers conclude that in John "the Jews" can mean the leaders, the people of Judea, or, as here, Jews who resist Jesus wherever they are; others, such as Steve Mason, translate the word "Judeans" throughout. The Plain English Translation keeps the word and does not narrow it.

a: This is Jesus, Joseph's son, isn't it?
p: The crowd knows his family. John never tells the story of Jesus's birth.
b: Philip also called Jesus "son of Joseph" (1:45). The crowd argues that a man whose parents they know cannot have come from heaven. John's readers know the irony: his true origin is from above (1:14; 3:31). Did John know the virgin birth told by Matthew and Luke? Some think so and see irony here, as in 7:41–42, where the crowd thinks Jesus comes from Galilee and not Bethlehem. Others think John simply did not use the tradition. John does not settle it. His concern is a deeper origin: the Word who was with God.

a: unless the Father who sent me draws him
p: Helkyō means to pull or drag. Whether God's drawing can be resisted divides churches.
b: The verb is used of hauling a net full of fish (21:6, 11), drawing a sword (18:10) and dragging people to court (Acts 16:19). It is strong. In the Greek of Jeremiah 31:3 (38:3 in the Septuagint), God says, "I have drawn you with mercy." In 12:32 Jesus says that, lifted up, he "will draw all people" to himself. Augustine wrote that the Father draws not by force but by delight, as a branch draws a sheep. Calvinist readers see a drawing that always succeeds; Arminian, Wesleyan, Catholic and Orthodox readers see a drawing that can be refused, offered to all (12:32). See the card "Where Christians differ."

a: 'And all of them will be taught by God.'
p: Jesus quotes Isaiah's promise for restored Zion, where all Zion's children will be the LORD's learners.
b: This site's Plain English Translation of Isaiah 54:13 reads: "All your children will be the LORD's learners, / and your children's peace will be great" (Isaiah 54:13). The Hebrew limmudim, "learners," is the word the Greek Old Testament renders didaktoi, "taught," and John's wording follows the Greek, dropping "your children" and saying simply "all." The promise belongs to the new covenant hope of Jeremiah 31:33–34, when no one will need to teach a neighbor to know the LORD. Jesus uses it to explain 6:44: God's drawing is God's teaching, and those who truly learn from the Father come to Jesus. "The Prophets" is a name for a section of Scripture, not one book.

a: Only the one who comes from God has seen the Father.
p: Hearing and learning from the Father (6:45) is not the same as seeing him. Only the Son has.
b: Jesus guards against a misunderstanding of 6:45. Being taught by God does not mean anyone has seen God. The LORD told Moses, "no human being can see me and stay alive" (Exodus 33:20). The prologue said that no one has ever seen God, and that the Son has made him known (1:18). So God's teaching comes through the one who has seen him.

a: the bread I will give is my flesh, for the sake of the world's life
p: John says "flesh," not "body" as at the Last Supper. "For" is the language of a death on behalf of others.
b: The Last Supper in Matthew, Mark, Luke and Paul has "this is my body" (sōma). John has sarx, "flesh," the word of 1:14, where the Word became flesh. Some scholars think John's wording reflects the Aramaic Jesus used at the Supper, which may have been "flesh" (bisra); Ignatius of Antioch also speaks of the Eucharist as Jesus's flesh. "For" (hyper) is the word John uses for Jesus's death on behalf of others (10:11, 15; 11:50–52; 15:13). So the future "I will give" points to the cross. From here the discourse moves from believing to eating.
orig: ἡ σάρξ μού ἐστιν ὑπὲρ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου ζωῆς

a: How is this man able to give us his flesh to eat?
p: To Jewish hearers, eating flesh and drinking blood sounded like cannibalism and broke a basic food law.
b: The Law forbade all eating of blood: "Only, flesh with its life, its blood, you must not eat" (Genesis 9:4), and Leviticus 17:10 warns of being cut off for it. The early church kept the ban for Gentile believers too (Acts 15:20, 29). So the hearers' shock is natural, and John keeps the offense rather than softening it. Outsiders later accused Christians of cannibalism because of their meal of "body and blood"; about AD 112 Pliny the Younger, a Roman governor, reported that Christians said they ate "ordinary and harmless food."

a: if you do not eat the Son of Man's flesh and drink his blood
t: What does eating his flesh mean?
p: Is this the Lord's Supper, believing in Jesus, or both? Christians have answered differently for centuries.
b: Readers fall into three broad groups. Many, especially Catholic and Orthodox Christians, read 6:51–58 as Jesus's teaching on the Eucharist, where believers really receive his body and blood. Others, including Luther, Calvin and most Protestant commentators, read it as a vivid picture of believing in Jesus and his death, since 6:35, 40 and 47 give eternal life to the one who believes, with words very like 6:54. Many modern scholars, Catholic and Protestant, take a middle view: the discourse is about faith in the crucified Jesus, and John's readers would also have heard their Supper in it. See the card "Where Christians differ" on this chapter's page.

a: Anyone who is eating my flesh
p: From 6:54 John switches to trōgō, a word that first meant to chew or munch.
b: Up to 6:53 the verb is the ordinary phagein. In 6:54, 56, 57 and 58 John uses trōgō, which in older Greek meant to gnaw or munch, as animals do. Some scholars think the change makes the language more physical, to rule out a purely spiritual meaning. Others note that by John's time trōgō had become a common present tense of "eat" (it appears again in 13:18, quoting Psalm 41:9), so the change is only grammar. The Plain English Translation says "eating," and this note gives the stronger sense.

a: remains in me, and I remain in him
p: "Remain" (menō) is one of John's key words: the lasting bond between Jesus and believers.
b: Menō means to remain, stay or live in a place. In John it describes the Spirit remaining on Jesus (1:32), the disciples staying with him (1:39), and above all the shared life of chapter 15, where Jesus tells the disciples to remain in him as he remains in them (15:4). Here that bond is tied to eating and drinking him. The Plain English Translation uses "remain" wherever John means this lasting bond (1:32; 3:36; 5:38; 6:27; 6:56; 8:31; 15:4–10) so the thread can be followed, and "stay" only for staying in a place (1:39).
orig: ἐν ἐμοὶ μένει κἀγὼ ἐν αὐτῷ

a: in a synagogue at Capernaum
p: Visitors today see a white limestone synagogue from the 300s–400s AD. An older building lies under it.
b: Capernaum was a fishing town on the north shore of the lake and Jesus's base in Galilee (Mark 2:1; Matthew 4:13). Its well-known synagogue, of white limestone, was dated by its Franciscan excavators to about AD 400; others date it to the 200s–300s. Under it, excavators found walls of black basalt that may belong to an earlier synagogue, perhaps the one Jesus knew. Luke says a centurion, probably a Gentile officer serving Herod Antipas, built the town's synagogue (Luke 7:5). The Greek here has no "the": "in synagogue," which may mean "in an assembly," during the Sabbath meeting.

a: This word is harsh.
p: Many disciples leave. Only the Twelve remain, and Peter speaks for them.
b: Sklēros means hard, rough or harsh: not hard to understand but hard to accept. This scene is John's version of a crisis the other Gospels also tell. In Mark, after the feedings, Jesus asks the disciples who they say he is, Peter names him the Messiah (Mark 8:27–30), and then Peter rebukes Jesus and is called Satan (Mark 8:33). In John the order is like Mark's: a feeding, a sea crossing, a demand for a sign, a confession by Peter, and a disciple called a devil, but here the devil is Judas (6:70).

a: So what if you see the Son of Man going up
p: Jesus does not finish the thought: "what if you see the Son of Man going up?" He leaves it to the hearers.
b: The Greek gives only the "if" half of a sentence. It can mean: "If this offends you, what will you think when you see me go up? It will be still harder." Or: "When you see me go up, then you will understand that I came down from heaven." In John, "going up" is reached through the cross, the "lifting up" (3:13–14; 12:32–33), and then the return to the Father (20:17). So the offense of flesh and blood will be followed by the greater offense, and the explanation, of the cross.

a: The flesh is of no use at all.
p: After "eat my flesh," Jesus says "the flesh is of no use." Readers have used the verse on both sides of the Supper debate.
b: Huldrych Zwingli made this verse his main argument against the real presence of Christ's body in the Supper: if flesh profits nothing, eating it bodily cannot be the point. Luther answered that "the flesh" here does not mean Christ's flesh, but human nature and understanding, and Catholic interpreters since John Chrysostom have said the same: the hearers took Jesus in a fleshly way, as if he meant cutting up his body. Many commentators hear John's contrast of flesh and Spirit from 3:6: human nature alone cannot grasp or receive this life; the Spirit gives it, through Jesus's words. The Plain English Translation capitalizes the first "Spirit" as God's Spirit and writes the second "spirit" in lowercase, since Jesus's sayings are spiritual in nature; the Greek has no capitals, and some translations make both lowercase.

a: which one would hand him over
p: The verb means to hand over. In the Gospels it is the regular word for what Judas did.
b: Paradidōmi literally means "hand over, deliver up." English Bibles usually say "betray" when it is used of Judas, because his handing over was treachery. The same verb is used when the Jewish leaders hand Jesus over to Pilate (18:30, 35) and Pilate hands him over to be crucified (19:16), and Paul uses it of God, who "handed him over" for us (Romans 8:32). The Plain English Translation keeps "hand over" so readers can see the chain.

a: Lord, who would we go to?
p: This is John's version of Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi.
b: In Matthew Peter names Jesus the Messiah and the Son of the living God (Matthew 16:16); in Mark, the Messiah (Mark 8:29); in Luke, God's Messiah (Luke 9:20). John's Peter speaks in the language of this chapter: Jesus has "the sayings of eternal life" (compare 6:63). His answer is not a theory but a choice: there is nowhere else to go. Later copyists made his words here match Matthew (see the variant at 6:69).

a: God's Holy One
p: In Mark a demon gives Jesus this title. In the Old Testament the priest Aaron is "the LORD's holy one."
b: "Holy One of God" is rare. In Mark 1:24 and Luke 4:34 an unclean spirit shouts that it knows who Jesus is, God's Holy One. Psalm 106:16 calls Aaron "the LORD's holy one," and God himself is often "the Holy One of Israel" in Isaiah. In John the Father has "set apart" the Son and sent him (10:36), and Jesus sets himself apart for his disciples (17:19). The title says Jesus belongs wholly to God.
orig: ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ (ho hagios tou theou)

a: one of you is a devil
p: Diabolos means slanderer or accuser. Jesus calls one of his chosen Twelve by the name of the enemy.
b: Elsewhere in the New Testament ho diabolos is the devil himself. Without "the," it can mean an accuser or slanderer (1 Timothy 3:11). Jesus is not saying Judas is a demon in disguise. He says that one of the Twelve already serves the enemy's purpose. Later John says the devil put the plan into Judas's heart (13:2) and Satan entered him (13:27). In Mark, after Peter's confession, it is Peter whom Jesus calls Satan (Mark 8:33).

a: Judas, son of Simon Iscariot
p: Most likely "man of Kerioth," a town in Judea. Other guesses tie it to daggers or to falsehood.
b: John alone says Judas's father was also called Iscariot (also 13:2, 26), so it seems to be a family name, probably from a place. The most common view is Hebrew ish Qeriyyot, "man of Kerioth," a town in southern Judea (Joshua 15:25 names a Kerioth-hezron). That would make Judas the only Judean among the Twelve. One manuscript tradition here reads "from Kerioth" (see the variant). Other suggestions are sicarius, "dagger man," a name for Jewish rebels, or a word for "liar" or "one who hands over." None is certain.
